lines: It's an account secured too late.
scenes.sub: This lesson closes every door, in order, before money is ever at risk.
scenes.vo: Here's why this lesson comes before you buy anything. The single biggest reason a beginner's first crypto experience goes wrong isn't a bad trade. It's an account that was funded before it was secured: a weak password, no two-factor, a phone number that can be hijacked. Every step in this lesson closes one of those doors, in order, before money is ever at risk.

scenes.title: What this lesson covers

items.title: Choosing an exchange
items.text: What to look for, and why

scenes.vo: Here's the plan. First, what an exchange actually is, and how to choose one. Second, the six-step lockdown that comes before any money goes in. Third, Maria's worked example, start to finish. And finally, your checklist and a quick quiz.

Here's the idea in one picture. An exchange is your on-ramp from ordinary money into crypto. But before you send it a single dollar, you lock the account down. Order matters: account, then security, then money.

scenes.title: What to look for
scenes.sub: Licensed, established, and it supports what you need.
scenes.vo: Choosing an exchange.

scenes.sub: It swaps ordinary money for crypto. That's the whole job.
scenes.vo: First, what an exchange even is. It's a company that lets you swap ordinary money, dollars, pounds, euros, for crypto. It's your on-ramp, not your final destination.

scenes.title: The sign-up sequence
scenes.vo: Here's the sign-up sequence you'll actually go through. You create the account with an email and a password. You verify that email address. You complete K.Y.C., uploading your I.D. and sometimes a proof of address. And once that's approved, the account is ready, but not yet secured. That's the part most beginners rush past, and it's the whole subject of the next chapter.

That's the part most beginners rush past, and it's the whole subject of the next chapter.

scenes.title: Three things to check

items.title: Supports what you need
items.text: Your bank, plus ETH, USDC, low-cost networks

scenes.vo: Choose one that's licensed or registered where you live, check your country's financial regulator. Large and long-established, with a good security record. And one that supports your bank's deposit method, plus the coins and networks you'll actually use, like E.T.H., U.S.D.C., and low-cost networks such as Arbitrum or Base. Well-known examples include Coinbase, Kraken, Binance, Bybit and O.K.X., but availability differs by country, so pick one that's legally available to you.

And one that supports your bank's deposit method, plus the coins and networks you'll actually use, like ETH, USDC, and low-cost networks such as Arbitrum or Base. Well-known examples include Coinbase, Kraken, Binance, Bybit and OKX, but availability differs by country, so pick one that's legally available to you.

scenes.sub: A regulated exchange asking for this is a good sign, not a red flag.
scenes.vo: You'll also be asked for K.Y.C., know your customer: your ID, and sometimes proof of address. This is normal, and it's legally required for a regulated exchange. Treat a request for it as a good sign, not a red flag.
scenes.cap: You'll also be asked for KYC, know your customer: your ID, and sometimes proof of address. This is normal, and it's legally required for a regulated exchange. Treat a request for it as a good sign, not a red flag.

scenes.title: Reputable exchange vs. red flag
scenes.vo: So flip those three checks around, and you get the red flags. A reputable exchange is licensed, has a long track record, and asks for K.Y.C. A red-flag one is unregistered anywhere you can verify, brand new with no history, and skips identity checks entirely, which sounds convenient but is actually a warning sign, not a shortcut.
scenes.cap: So flip those three checks around, and you get the red flags. A reputable exchange is licensed, has a long track record, and asks for KYC. A red-flag one is unregistered anywhere you can verify, brand new with no history, and skips identity checks entirely, which sounds convenient but is actually a warning sign, not a shortcut.

scenes.sub: Even large exchanges have had outages and incidents. This isn't a guarantee that nothing ever goes wrong.
scenes.vo: One caution, though. Choosing a licensed, reputable exchange doesn't mean zero risk. Even large, well-known exchanges have had outages and security incidents. It means a far better starting point, and someone accountable if something goes wrong, not a guarantee that nothing ever will.

scenes.title: Before you type a password
steps: Type the address yourself, or use a saved bookmark
Check the domain matches, letter for letter
Never log in via a link from an email, text or ad
scenes.result: A fake site can't steal what you never type into it.
scenes.vo: One habit protects you before any of the lockdown steps even apply: making sure you're actually on the real site. Type the address yourself, or use a bookmark you saved the first time. Check the domain matches, letter for letter, not just something that looks close. Look for the padlock. And never log in by following a link from an email, a text, or a search ad, even if it looks exactly right.

scenes.title: Before you deposit a cent
scenes.sub: Do all six. In this order.
scenes.vo: The six-step lockdown.

scenes.title: Why order matters
scenes.vo: Here's why the order matters, using the first step as the example. Skip securing your email, and this is the chain that can follow. Someone breaks into your email, often with a password leaked from another site entirely. They click forgot password on your exchange. The reset link lands in the email they now control. And they set a new exchange password, before you even notice. Lock the email first, and this whole chain breaks at step one.

scenes.title: The must-do basics

nodes.label: Secure your email first
nodes.sub: It can reset your exchange too

scenes.vo: Here's the first half, the must-do basics. Step one, secure your email first, because whoever controls it can often reset your exchange account too. Step two, a unique, long password for the exchange itself, stored in a password manager. And step three, two-factor authentication with an authenticator app or a hardware security key, not text messages.
scenes.cap: Here's the first half, the must-do basics. Step one, secure your email first, because whoever controls it can often reset your exchange account too. Step two, a unique, long password for the exchange itself, stored in a password manager. And step three, two-factor authentication with an authenticator app or a hardware security key, not text messages.

scenes.title: Text codes vs. an authenticator

left.label: SMS codes
items: A SIM swap sends them to a criminal

right.label: App or hardware key
items: Stays on a device you hold
Can't be redirected by a phone company

scenes.vo: Why not text messages? Because a criminal can talk your phone company into moving your number to their SIM card, a SIM swap, and your codes go straight to them. An authenticator app, or a hardware key, never leaves your possession.
scenes.cap: Why not text messages? Because a criminal can talk your phone company into moving your number to their SIM card, a SIM swap, and your codes go straight to them. An authenticator app, or a hardware key, never leaves your possession.

scenes.title: How a SIM swap actually works
scenes.vo: Here's exactly how a SIM swap works, because the mechanism is what makes it dangerous. The attacker calls your phone company, posing as you, often using personal details found elsewhere. They convince the company to move your number onto a SIM card they control. Your phone loses signal, usually without much warning. And every text message, including your two-factor codes, now arrives on their phone instead of yours.

scenes.title: The extra armour

nodes.label: Anti-phishing code
nodes.sub: A word only real emails carry

scenes.vo: Here's the second half, the extra armour most beginners skip. Step four, save your two-factor backup codes offline, on paper, somewhere safe. Step five, turn on the anti-phishing code if it's offered, a word that appears in every genuine email the exchange sends you. And step six, turn on the withdrawal address allowlist if it's offered, so withdrawals can only ever go to addresses you've pre-approved.

Step five, turn on the anti-phishing code if it's offered, a word that appears in every genuine email the exchange sends you. And step six, turn on the withdrawal address allowlist if it's offered, so withdrawals can only ever go to addresses you've pre-approved.

scenes.q: What does a withdrawal allowlist do?
scenes.a: It restricts withdrawals to addresses you've pre-approved in advance, even if the account is later hijacked.
scenes.vo: Quick check. What does a withdrawal allowlist actually do? [[pause 4]] The answer: it restricts withdrawals so they can only go to addresses you've pre-approved, so even a hijacked account can't send funds somewhere new.

scenes.title: Twenty minutes, start to finish
scenes.sub: Ten for KYC, ten for security.
scenes.vo: Maria's worked example.

scenes.title: Maria's setup, twenty minutes
scenes.note: Security is half the job, not an afterthought.
scenes.vo: Here's exactly where Maria's twenty minutes goes. Ten minutes on K.Y.C., signing up and verifying who she is. And ten more on security: a password manager, authenticator-app two-factor on both her email and the exchange, backup codes on paper, and an anti-phishing code. Security isn't the slow part. It's half the job, and it's the half most beginners skip.

scenes.title: Maria's setup
steps: Backup codes written down, stored safely
Turns on the withdrawal address allowlist
scenes.result: Twenty minutes. All six steps done before a deposit.
scenes.vo: Now the whole thing, step by step. Maria signs up, and completes K.Y.C. in about ten minutes. She installs a password manager, and gives the exchange a unique password. She turns on authenticator-app two-factor, on both her email and the exchange. She writes her backup codes on paper, and stores them safely. And she sets an anti-phishing code: the word “blue-kettle.”

scenes.title: Why the anti-phishing code works

nodes.label: You choose a word
nodes.sub: Only you and the exchange know it

scenes.vo: Here's why that one word works so well. You choose it yourself, when you turn the feature on, and only you and the exchange ever know it. Every genuine email the exchange sends you includes it, somewhere in the text. An attacker writing a fake email has no way to know what word you picked. So a missing code isn't a minor detail. It's the whole tell.

scenes.sub: One missing word, and the whole attack fails.
scenes.vo: A few weeks later, an email arrives: “suspicious login, verify your account now.” It looks right. Same logo, same layout. But it doesn't say “blue-kettle” anywhere. Maria knows instantly it's fake, and deletes it without clicking a thing.

scenes.sub: The six steps work just as well on an account you opened last year.
scenes.vo: One more thing, if you already opened an exchange account before this lesson. Everything here still applies to it. Go back now, and work through all six lockdown steps on that account, before you do anything else with it.

scenes.title: Confirm you've got it

scenes.title: Before you deposit
items: Exchange chosen: legal and reputable where you live
Exchange 2FA: app or key, never SMS
scenes.vo: Here's this lesson's checklist. Exchange chosen: legally available and reputable where you live. K.Y.C. complete. Email secured with its own strong password and two-factor. Exchange two-factor via an authenticator app or security key, never S.M.S. Backup codes stored offline. And the anti-phishing code and withdrawal allowlist switched on, if your exchange offers them.

scenes.q: An email claiming to be from your exchange is missing your anti-phishing code. What should you do?
scenes.a: Treat it as fake. Don't click anything in it, and delete it — the missing code is the tell.
